text: Three hundred years ago, one place on Earth made about a quarter of everything the whole world produced.
Not Britain. Not China. Not America.
India.‡
Spices, cotton, steel, diamonds. Ships came from the other side of the planet just to buy what India made.
[checking his pocket watch, impressed] Richest shop on the planet. And it was always open.
India was so rich, people had a name for it: Sone ki Chidiya. The Golden Bird.
[nervous] And when you're a golden bird... everyone wants to catch you.
Then, in less than two hundred and fifty years... that quarter shrank to about four percent.‡
[winces] Ah. Someone forgot to lock the shop.
And here's the strange part. This wasn't the first time. India has been rich... and robbed... and rebuilt... again and again, for five thousand years.
Over that time, this land was ruled by city-builders nobody can name, an emperor who gave up war after one terrible battle, sultans, Mughals, a company... and finally, its own people.
[nervous] A company. I'll explain later. You will not believe it.
Because if you look closely, India keeps living the same story.
First, someone stitches the land together. Then it shines, the richest place on Earth. Then it shatters into pieces. Outsiders march in to take it...
...and then something strange happens. India absorbs them. The invaders end up eating its food, speaking its languages, and building its monuments.
Stitch. Shine. Shatter. Absorb. Again and again.
So how did one land become the richest place in the world, lose it all, and start climbing back?
[winding his watch] Hold on to something.
Let's go back to the very beginning.
About forty-five hundred years ago, while Egypt was building its pyramids, a civilisation was growing along the Indus River, in what is today Pakistan and northwest India.
We call it the Indus Valley Civilisation. And it was huge. It covered more land than Egypt and Mesopotamia put together.
Its biggest cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, were home to tens of thousands of people.
And these cities were... weirdly modern.
Streets ran in neat, straight lines. Houses were built from bricks of the same size, everywhere, for hundreds of years.
Many houses had their own bathroom. Wastewater flowed into covered drains under the street.
[looking down at a drain, stunned] Four and a half thousand years ago. Underground drainage.
[to camera] Some cities today are still working on this.
In the middle of Mohenjo-daro sat something archaeologists call the Great Bath. A brick pool, sealed with tar so it wouldn't leak.
Nobody knows exactly what it was for. Maybe ceremonies. Maybe a very fancy swimming pool.
[holding up the brick] What is this?
A brick, sir. A nice brick.
It's bigger. One to two to four. Every brick. Every city. Every time.
[quietly] I was trying to be creative.
[hands it back] Be creative with pots.
They even used standard weights for trading, so nobody got cheated at the market.
And they traded far. Indus seals have been found all the way in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq.
But here's the mystery.
These people wrote. On seals, on pots, on tags. Hundreds of different signs.
And nobody can read them. Not one word. To this day.
[squinting at a seal with a unicorn-like animal] Fish. Jar. Unicorn. [shrugs] Either a king's name or a grocery list.
So we don't know what they called themselves. We don't know their kings, their gods, or their stories.
Oddly, archaeologists haven't found grand palaces or giant royal tombs either. Just well-planned cities, built for ordinary people.
Then, around nineteen hundred BCE, the great cities slowly emptied.
Why? Nobody knows for sure. Historians suspect a mix: rivers changing course, a river drying up, and the monsoon growing weaker for years.
People drifted east and south into smaller villages. The drains filled with mud. The cities were forgotten.
For almost four thousand years.
And how did the world rediscover them? Through a railway.
In the eighteen-fifties, British engineers were building a railway line in Punjab. They needed lots of bricks.
And near a village called Harappa, they found a huge pile of old, perfect bricks just lying in the ground.
Sir, there's an old ruin full of bricks over there.
[delighted] Free bricks? Splendid. Old ruins never matter.
[face in his hands] They matter. They really, really matter.
Bricks from a four-thousand-year-old city ended up under the tracks.
Only in the nineteen-twenties did archaeologists realise what they were digging up: one of the oldest civilisations on Earth.
So that was India's first shine. Rich, organised, connected to the world.
And then, its first shatter. Its cities fell silent.
[making a note] Loop step one. Check.
But the land didn't stay empty for long. Over the mountains in the northwest, new people were coming. They brought horses, chariots...
...and a collection of hymns so sacred, it was passed down word for word, by memory alone, for more than three thousand years.
[watch ticking, leaning in] Now this one, people still argue about.
